subject: Discrepancy in plots between pairs.stanfit and shinystan

messages.author: 395bdca538bcae5d
messages.subject: Discrepancy in plots between pairs.stanfit and shinystan
parts:
I've been using shinystan to explore my model (very helpful, thank you) and noticed that it shows the divergent transitions in different locations than the pairs() plots.

I've doubled checked twice now and something is amiss. The shinystan one seems right, as I'd expect from a centered parameterization it's giving divergences at the small end of the "funnel." I've attached the two plots.

Is this a bug or am I doing something wrong? Code used to generate below..

Thanks,
Cole

stan.swallows.fit <-
  stan(file='models/swallows/swallows.stan', par=pars.swallows,
       init=inits.swallows.fn, data=data.swallows, iter=2000,
       chains=ncores, control=list(adapt_delta=.8))
my_sso <- shinystan::launch_shinystan(stan.swallows.fit)
png('pairs_swallows.png', res=500, width=7, height=5, units='in')
pairs(stan.swallows.fit, pars=c('sigmayearphi', 'yeareffphi[1]'))
dev.off()

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Discrepancy in plots between pairs.stanfit and shinystan
parts:
Thanks. We should definitely make those consistent.

As Michael just wrote to our users list, it's tricky because we
only plot one point and it's the entire trajectory that diverges.
The divergence in question is when the Hamiltonian, which is supposed
to remain constant, gets far away from its initial value during
leapfrog integration (due to numerical issues of not having a small
enough step size and the gradient with small step sizes not being
very good in highly curved volumes of the posterior).

from Michael Betancourt:

> It’s not the initial point that is shown, but the point sampled from the
> trajectory prior to proposing the new subtree with the divergence.
> It’s still not exactly where the divergence occurred, but it can be closer
> than the initial point. Also, a divergence is technically a property of
> the trajectory and not a single point, so it can be difficult to track back
> and blame a single point even if the entire trajectory was saved.

- Bob
